pages.title: The Art of Writing
pages.text: Writing a stable Age requires strict grammar. The golden rule is simple: $(c)modifiers must precede the thing they modify.$() $(br)$(br)Examples: color pages go before the color target, and a rare $(thing)Age Effect$() page goes before the chosen potion effect page.

pages.title: Grammar Leaks
pages.text: A grammar leak happens when a modifier is written without a destination. A custom color with no color target, or an Age Effect page with no effect page after it, leaves the compiler guessing. That guess is never good for stability.

pages.title: Contradictions
pages.text: Conflicting absolutes tear the fabric of an Age apart. Writing $(c)Fast Time$() and $(c)Slow Time$() together, or multiple terrain identities that fight each other, stacks heavy instability even if the book still compiles.

pages.title: Stable Basics
pages.text: If you want a calmer Age, define the basics: $(li)terrain$(li)biomes$(li)time$(li)sun$(li)moon$(li)stars$(li)weather$() $(br)Simple, explicit Ages are safer than sparse ones, and a clearly authored single-biome Age is especially stable.

pages.title: The Wildcard
pages.text: Including a $(c)Random$() page forces the universe to fill in blanks with chaos. Random Ages are far more likely to roll exotic landmarks, historic remains, rare oddities, and higher instability.
